tldr: By combining a Flow Matching motion generator that plans whole-body trajectories from raw depth images with a high-speed tracking policy, and fine-tuning the generator via off-policy RL (AWR), a humanoid robot traverses stairs, jumps on boxes, and sprints outdoors at 2 m/s without any odometry.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed pipeline: dynamically optimized human MoCap data builds a terrain-consistent motion library, CLF-RL trains the tracking policy, a depth-conditioned Flow Matching motion generator is learned, and off-policy RL (AWR) fine-tunes the generator to improve terrain consistency.
overview:
To navigate diverse real-world environments, humanoids need the ability to seamlessly switch between varied skills—such as walking, running, climbing stairs, and jumping over obstacles—purely from visual feedback. However, most existing perceptive locomotion controllers are restricted to flat ground or rely heavily on expensive height maps and precise odometry, creating major bottlenecks for outdoor deployment and whole-body control.

To overcome this, the authors propose a hierarchical architecture that completely decouples motion generation from trajectory tracking. An upper-level motion generator uses Flow Matching to plan whole-body trajectories every 0.24 seconds from raw depth images and commanded velocities, while a lower-level tracking policy follows these motions at 50 Hz. The central breakthrough of this work is an off-policy reinforcement learning loop (AWR: Advantage Weighted Regression) that directly fine-tunes the upper-level motion generator while keeping the tracker fixed. Instead of performing naive exploration over the massive ~3,000-dimensional trajectory space per step, they introduce a structured search method that perturbs the generator's input noise and conditioning tokens.

Across simulation and real-world experiments on the Unitree G1 humanoid, RL fine-tuning boosted successful terrain traversals by up to 25 percentage points and improved skill selection accuracy by up to 80 percentage points. In hardware tests, without using any height maps or odometry and relying solely on onboard compute and two depth cameras, the robot reliably climbed outdoor stairs, jumped on boxes, and achieved turning sprints at over 7 km/h (2 m/s).
contributions: Built a hierarchical perceptive locomotion system combining a Flow Matching generator that outputs whole-body trajectories directly from raw depth images with a high-precision CLF-RL tracking policy

Proposed an off-policy RL fine-tuning loop that sample-efficiently improves a generative model with a ~3,000-dimensional trajectory output using structured search and Advantage Weighted Regression (AWR)

Developed an automated data pipeline using physical optimization and Motion Bricks on human MoCap data to produce 10,000 terrain-consistent motion clips with guaranteed periodicity and velocity accuracy

Demonstrated real-world outdoor stair traversal, jumping, and 2 m/s sprinting on a physical humanoid without any odometry or height maps, autonomously adjusting speed by anticipating obstacles with two depth cameras

sections.heading: Why does perceptive humanoid locomotion stumble in the real world?
sections.summary: For humanoids to operate in the real world, they must combine diverse dynamic skills with visual terrain perception. This paper adopts a decoupled generate-and-track architecture, aiming for versatile outdoor navigation across complex terrains using only raw depth camera inputs.
sections.details:
Building humanoids that can go anywhere humans can requires instantly switching between a wide variety of skills—walking, running, climbing stairs, and leaping across obstacles—based on the terrain immediately ahead.

However, most existing terrain-adaptive locomotion policies are tailored to a single speed or a specific gait, lacking extensibility to whole-body coordination or arbitrary velocity commands. On the other hand, while general-purpose whole-body tracking controllers capable of imitating diverse motions have emerged, they typically lack visual perception to sense the terrain and adapt their motions accordingly.

Another major obstacle lies in how robots perceive the external world. Prior works frequently rely on height maps, which require accurate odometry and complex scanning pipelines. These easily break down on real, shaking humanoid hardware deployed outdoors.

To solve these challenges, the authors adopt a two-layer hierarchy pairing a perceptive motion generator with a perceptive high-speed tracker. Furthermore, they introduce a framework to reinforce the generator itself with RL so that it intelligently selects the right motions even on unseen terrains.

sections.heading: Limitations of prior work and the new concept of RL-fine-tuned generators
sections.summary: While imitation learning and diffusion-based motion generation have gained traction in humanoid control, coordinating generators with trackers and achieving online adaptation remain challenging. This work stands apart by directly fine-tuning the motion generator via off-policy RL.
sections.details:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has become mainstream in humanoid control, where mimic-style methods that track human MoCap references have driven the acquisition of natural, lifelike behaviors.

### Motion Tracking and Perceptive Approaches
While progress has been made in giving tracking controllers arbitrary velocity commands or embedding simplified models, visual integration remains divided. Approaches that build elevation maps are often bottlenecked by state estimation drift, whereas end-to-end methods that process camera depth directly face observability and compute hurdles.

### State of Generator-Tracker Architectures
Hierarchical frameworks that generate kinematic trajectories at the top level and track them physically at the lower level have attracted recent interest. However, prior work like SONIC was limited to flat ground without vision, and diffusion-based methods like PARC were simulation-only and required nearly a month to train, falling far short of real-world deployment. Moreover, methods that only fine-tune the lower-level tracker cannot recover if the upper-level generator chooses an entirely wrong behavior (e.g., executing a flat walk on stairs).

### RL Fine-Tuning of Generative Models
Fine-tuning diffusion models or Flow Matching with RL has begun in robotic manipulation, but most efforts target low-dimensional arm action spaces or freeze the generator while learning a residual policy. This work is the first to directly update the weights of the motion generator itself on an extremely high-dimensional output space of dynamic whole-body locomotion trajectories.

sections.heading: System overview: A four-stage pipeline from data optimization to RL fine-tuning
sections.summary: The proposed system consists of four stages: data creation, tracker training, generator training, and generator RL fine-tuning. On hardware, a 26.8M-parameter Flow Matching generator works in tandem with a lightweight MLP tracking policy.
sections.details:
The proposed workflow consists of the four steps illustrated in Figure F2.

- **Division of Roles**: The upper-level Generator plans a 1.24-second whole-body trajectory every 0.24 seconds (12 control steps), while the lower-level Tracker computes joint torques at 50 Hz (0.02-second intervals) to drive the robot.
- **Decoupled Perception and Compute**: The tracker quickly balances using proprioception (joint states, etc.) and a downward-facing camera depth image, while the generator formulates global plans using velocity commands and two camera views. This compute decoupling maintains strict real-time control while running an expressive generative model.

captions.F2: Overall flow of the proposed system: human MoCap data is optimized to build a motion library, and the tracker is trained with CLF-RL. Next, the Flow Matching generator is trained on depth images collected from tracking rollouts, and finally, the generator is fine-tuned with off-policy RL (AWR).

sections.heading: A data pipeline that physically refines human motion
sections.summary: Raw human MoCap data cannot be directly tracked by a robot. By combining multiple-shooting state-constrained optimization in MuJoCo with Motion Bricks, the authors created 10,000 physically consistent motion clips.
sections.details:
Creating a high-quality motion library sets the performance ceiling for the entire framework.

### Extracting Periodic Trajectories via Physics Optimization
From an open-source human motion dataset (bones-seed), the authors extracted 252 flat-ground motions (forward, backward, turning, sidestepping, sprinting) and 46 obstacle motions (box jumping and stair climbing). Using a multiple-shooting formulation that incorporates MuJoCo contact dynamics differentiably, they slightly modify contact schedules while strictly solving for trajectories that satisfy both periodic boundary constraints (matching initial and final states) and average velocity constraints.

### Terrain Adaptation and Clip Synthesis with Motion Bricks
Because the raw MoCap lacks accurate terrain information, terrain was introduced into the simulation, contact forces were thresholded to obtain foot contact schedules, and motions were geometrically retargeted across various step heights. Running physics optimization again yielded motions that smoothly negotiate varied steps.

Finally, to seamlessly connect these base behaviors, the generative model Motion Bricks was used to synthesize transition clips. This automatically constructed a library of 10,000 clips (each 6 to 20 seconds long) across 140 terrain tiles.

sections.heading: Training a robust tracking policy guided by control theory
sections.summary: To accurately track generated trajectories, the authors use CLF-RL, integrating Control Lyapunov Functions into RL. The policy takes proprioception and coarse depth images and is trained at massive scale in IsaacLab.
sections.details:
The tracking controller adopts CLF-RL, known for high tracking precision and stability.

### Network Architecture and I/O
The tracker is a feedforward MLP operating at 50 Hz. It comprises a reference subnetwork (hidden layers: [1024, 512, 512]) processing future trajectories and commanded velocities, and a main network (hidden layers: [1024, 512, 256, 128]) integrating joint states and ultra-low-resolution depth images (30x26 pixels) from the downward camera. The output specifies target joint positions for joint PD controllers.

### Sim-to-Real and Training Environment
To ensure zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, extensive domain randomizations were applied to center of mass, joint friction, ground restitution, and camera mount angles. Using NVIDIA IsaacLab, training was performed across 8,192 parallel environments for approximately 48 hours using PPO on a single H100 GPU.

sections.heading: Vision-driven whole-body trajectory generator using Flow Matching
sections.summary: The motion generator is a Flow Matching Transformer that autoregressively predicts whole-body trajectories from dual-camera depth images and velocity commands. Inputting gravity-aligned 3D point cloud features enables terrain perception without odometry.
sections.details:
The high-level motion generator is a Flow Matching Transformer with 26.8M parameters.

### Input Representation: Gravity-Aligned Coordinates
The generator receives neither odometry (state estimation) nor proprioceptive joint angles. Instead, it processes dual-camera depth streams (5 channels per pixel: raw depth, gravity-aligned 3D coordinates $x, y, z$ relative to the robot's base root, and a valid flag), converted into feature tokens via CNNs. Providing these gravity-aligned 3D coordinates is critical: without them, the network cannot distinguish whether the robot is pitching forward or an uphill slope is approaching.

### Accelerating Training and Inference
The authors collected a dataset of 200,000 steps by rolling out the tracker in simulation and applied terrain-relative positional data augmentations. At inference time, caching the Prefix Encoder representations enables the 8-step Euler integration of Flow Matching to finish in just 11 ms, comfortably fitting inside the 0.24-second replanning budget.

sections.heading: Searching a 3,000-dimensional action space: Generator fine-tuning with AWR
sections.summary: Pretrained generators can fail on unseen terrains or complex skill transitions. By using structured search via conditioning perturbations and Advantage Weighted Regression (AWR) with a frozen tracker, the generator becomes substantially smarter.
sections.details:
Even a well-pretrained generator can fail when confronted with unfamiliar stair dimensions or composite tasks like jumping onto a box and immediately jumping down. The core highlight of this paper is the RL fine-tuning loop designed to resolve this (Figure F3).

### High-Dimensional Action Space and Structured Search
The whole-body trajectory produced by the generator in a single planning cycle spans 62 nodes x 44 dimensions = 2,728 dimensions (~3,000 dimensions). Applying standard PPO with naive Gaussian noise over this massive output space simply causes incoherent joint vibrations rather than meaningful exploration.

Instead, the authors introduce a structured search method that injects perturbations into the inputs—specifically, the initial Flow Matching noise and conditioning tokens such as velocity commands. This allows the system to efficiently explore physically coherent, natural motion candidates across distinct behavioral modes (e.g., leaping across vs. taking small climbing steps).

### Supervised Off-Policy Updates via AWR
A value function (Critic) is trained on collected rollouts using Fitted Value Iteration (FVI), estimating advantages $A(s, a) = R(s, a) - V(s)$. Behaviors yielding higher advantages receive larger weights $w = \min\{\exp(\frac{1}{\beta} \tilde{A}), L\}$ in a weighted Flow Matching loss. Running this loop for just 5 iterations (5 epochs per iteration, roughly 6 hours on an H100) delivers substantial performance leaps.

captions.F3: Architecture of the RL Fine-Tuning loop for the generator. Rollout data is collected in simulation via perturbed conditioning, advantages are estimated with a Critic, and the generator weights are directly updated using advantage-weighted Flow Matching loss.

sections.heading: Hardware implementation on a physical humanoid
sections.summary: The Unitree G1 was equipped with NVIDIA Jetson Thor, Jetson Orin, and two Zed cameras for a fully self-contained onboard computing setup. With minimized latency, the robot is directly steered via a Bluetooth joystick.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on the Unitree G1 humanoid.

- **Onboard Compute**: High-level control and policy inference run on an NVIDIA Jetson Thor, while camera depth processing and downsampling are handled by an NVIDIA Jetson Orin. Both communicate over ROS2 and are powered entirely by the robot's onboard battery.
- **Camera Setup**: Two cameras are mounted: an upper Zed X on the chest looking ahead, and a lower Zed X mini on the lower torso looking down at the feet and legs.
- **Inference Latency**: On Thor, inference takes approximately 11 ms for the Flow Matching generator and under 1 ms for the tracker, keeping sensor-to-action latency extremely low.

sections.heading: Experimental findings: Triumphs on unseen terrain and real-world outdoor trials
sections.summary: RL fine-tuning boosted success rates by up to 25 percentage points and improved skill selection accuracy by up to 80 percentage points. In hardware tests without odometry, the robot conquered 6 different outdoor staircases, jumped on boxes, and sprinted outdoors at 7.2 km/h (2 m/s).
sections.details:
Comprehensive validations were performed in both simulation and real hardware.

### III-A & III-B RL Fine-Tuning and Algorithmic Comparisons
The impact of fine-tuning was evaluated in out-of-distribution (OOD) environments, including unseen step heights and walled stairs.
- **Performance Gains**: Overall terrain traversal success rates increased by up to 25 percentage points, while terrain contact penalties dropped significantly. Skill selection errors—such as mistakenly attempting a box jump on stairs—improved by up to 80 percentage points.
- **Algorithmic Comparisons**: Proposed AWR substantially outperformed Filtered Behavioral Cloning (Filtered BC) and Plain BC. Compared to a PPO residual policy baseline, PPO consumed over 160x more data and 30x more wall-clock time while still achieving 13 percentage points lower success, highlighting the exceptional sample efficiency of AWR.

### III-C & III-F Autonomous Speed Adjustment and Dual Cameras
A robot cannot sprint up stairs or boxes at full speed. As shown in Figure F6, the upper camera detects upcoming obstacles early; even if the operator commands a constant 2.2 m/s forward speed, the robot autonomously decelerates to around 0.8 m/s ahead of the obstacle, traverses it safely, and resumes commanded speed afterward. In ablation studies without the upper camera, the robot collided with obstacles without slowing down, causing success rates to drop by up to 43%.

### III-D Hardware Demonstrations
Hardware experiments with the Unitree G1 (Figure F7) were conducted in real outdoor environments rather than controlled indoor labs. The robot successfully traversed 6 different outdoor staircases (including a continuous 15-step flight), jumped onto and off boxes, and sprinted with turns at 2 m/s (7.2 km/h) on paved paths. Footfalls were remarkably quiet and smooth, without foot slapping.

captions.F6: Autonomous speed adjustment during terrain traversal. Even when commanded to run at high speeds such as 2.20 m/s (dashed line), the robot autonomously decelerates to a safe speed before obstacles and stairs, smoothly resuming the commanded speed once cleared.
captions.F7: Hardware validation on the Unitree G1 humanoid. The robot showcases dynamic skills including ascending and descending diverse outdoor stairs, jumping onto boxes, and sprint-turning at 2 m/s on outdoor pavement.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: Pairing a Flow Matching generator with a tracking policy and fine-tuning the generator with AWR achieves practical perceptive humanoid locomotion. Future directions include integrating semantic reasoning and learning directly from real-world data.
sections.details:
This work demonstrates that tightly coupling generative modeling, tracking control, and RL fine-tuning enables humanoids to traverse diverse real-world terrains.

### Current Limitations
The fine-tuning reward functions are manually designed and may not generalize across arbitrary new skills. Furthermore, relying purely on raw depth means the system lacks semantic understanding, such as distinguishing whether a box is safe to jump onto or is a fragile obstacle.

### Future Work
Future directions include closing the loop by fine-tuning the generator directly from real-world robot rollouts, as well as integrating high-level navigation and obstacle avoidance stacks.

sections.heading: Appendix: Scaled CLF-RL ensuring theoretical stability
sections.summary: To address numerical discrepancies between position and velocity errors in Control Lyapunov Function (CLF) tracking, a novel scaling matrix was introduced and proven to maintain theoretical stability guarantees.
sections.details:
In CLF-RL reward design, the solution $P$ to the Continuous Algebraic Riccati Equation (CARE) is used to guarantee exponential stability toward the reference trajectory.

However, in practice, velocity states exhibit much higher variance than position states, causing instability under standard weighting schemes. To address this, the authors introduced a diagonal scaling matrix $S$ into a modified Lyapunov function: $\bar{V}(\eta) = \eta^{\top} S P S \eta$.

In this appendix, they mathematically prove that $SPS$ is a valid positive definite stabilizing CARE solution for modified weight matrices $(\bar{Q}, \bar{R})$, providing rigorous theoretical backing that numerical tuning flexibility does not compromise exponential CLF stability.

takeaways: Fine-tuning the generator rather than the tracker with RL dramatically eliminates terrain-dependent skill mode selection errors
For massive ~3,000-dimensional trajectory planning, structured search perturbing generator noise and conditioning is far more effective than adding Gaussian noise to outputs
A dual-camera setup (forward-looking and downward-looking) enables intelligent autonomous deceleration ahead of obstacles regardless of commanded speed
Using gravity-aligned raw depth coordinates while discarding odometry and height maps is the key to robust outdoor sim-to-real transfer
limitations: Relying solely on depth perception prevents semantic and material reasoning, such as identifying whether a step is structurally safe to jump on or fragile
Human engineering is still required to design physical optimization objectives for the motion library and reward functions for RL fine-tuning
Direct self-improvement from online real-world hardware data has not yet been demonstrated; fine-tuning remains confined to simulation environments
